title: Model Evaluation
blurb: Tests computing and choosing metrics from confusion matrices, thresholds, ranked scores, probabilities and regression errors, and spotting when a good-looking number misleads.

ideas.title: The confusion matrix, accuracy and the accuracy paradox
Thresholds, error costs and the business metric gap
Probabilistic quality: log loss, Brier score, calibration
Regression metrics: MAE, RMSE, MAPE, R²

questions.prompt: A fraud model flags a legitimate transaction as fraud (fraud is the positive class). Which cell of the confusion matrix does this land in?
options: False negative, a Type II error or "missed it"
True negative, because the transaction was legitimate
False positive, a Type I error or "false alarm"
True positive, because the model raised a flag
questions.explanation: The prediction was positive (fraud) and the truth was negative (legitimate). That is a false positive, a Type I error. A false negative is the opposite: real fraud the model let through.

questions.prompt: Which metric answers "of everything that was actually positive, how many did the model catch"?
options: Precision, $TP/(TP+FP)$
Accuracy, $(TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN)$
Recall, $TP/(TP+FN)$
questions.explanation: Recall divides the caught positives by all actual positives, $TP+FN$. Precision divides by everything **predicted** positive, $TP+FP$. Mixing the two denominators is the most common slip.

questions.prompt: A classifier's decision threshold moves from 0.5 down to 0.3. What typically happens?
options: Both precision and recall rise
ROC-AUC rises because more positives are predicted
Recall rises and precision falls
Precision rises and recall falls
questions.explanation: A lower threshold predicts positive more often. More true positives are caught (recall up), and more false alarms get through (precision down). ROC-AUC does not change, because it summarises every threshold at once.

questions.prompt: A model has ROC-AUC = 0.5 on a test set. What does that mean?
options: Its precision and recall are both 0.5
It classifies half the test cases correctly at the 0.5 threshold
Its scores rank positives above negatives no better than chance
Its predicted probabilities are well calibrated
questions.explanation: ROC-AUC measures ranking quality across all thresholds. 1.0 is perfect ranking and 0.5 is random. It is not an accuracy at any threshold, and it says nothing about whether the probabilities are calibrated.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a classifier to be **well calibrated**?
options: Its ROC-AUC is above 0.9 on held-out data
Of cases given 70%, about 70% turn out positive
It predicts each class about equally often
It ranks every positive above every negative
questions.explanation: Calibration asks whether the stated probabilities match observed frequencies. A reliability diagram of a calibrated model lies on the diagonal. Good ranking (high ROC-AUC) is discrimination, a different property. A model can rank well and still be over- or under-confident.

questions.prompt: A regression model scores $R^2 = -0.3$ on a test set. What does that mean?
options: The value is impossible, so the metric must have a bug
It does worse than always predicting the mean of the test targets
It explains 30% of the variance, with errors in the opposite direction
The predictions are negatively correlated with the targets, so flipping their sign would give $R^2 = 0.3$
questions.explanation: $R^2 = 1 - SS_{res}/SS_{tot}$. A value below 0 means the squared errors exceed those of the flat "predict the mean" baseline. $R^2$ has no lower bound on test data, so a negative value is possible and not a bug.

questions.prompt:
A classifier is scored on 1,000 cases:

|   | Predicted positive | Predicted negative |
|---|---|---|
| Actual positive | 45 | 15 |
| Actual negative | 30 | 910 |

What is the accuracy? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: Accuracy $= (TP+TN)/N = (45 + 910)/1000 = 0.955$. Compare the baseline that always predicts negative: $(30 + 910)/1000 = 0.940$. The model catches 45 of 60 positives, yet beats the do-nothing baseline by only 1.5 points of accuracy.

questions.prompt:
A classifier is scored on 1,000 cases:

|   | Predicted positive | Predicted negative |
|---|---|---|
| Actual positive | 45 | 15 |
| Actual negative | 30 | 910 |

What is the F1 score? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: Precision $= 45/(45+30) = 0.600$. Recall $= 45/(45+15) = 0.750$. $F1 = 2PR/(P+R) = 2(0.6)(0.75)/1.35 = 0.667$. Compare that with the accuracy of 0.955 on the same matrix.

questions.prompt:
A classifier is scored on 1,000 cases:

|   | Predicted positive | Predicted negative |
|---|---|---|
| Actual positive | 45 | 15 |
| Actual negative | 30 | 910 |

Specificity is $TN/(TN+FP)$, the share of actual negatives correctly left alone. It equals $1 - \text{FPR}$, where FPR is the ROC curve's x-axis. What is the specificity? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: Specificity $= 910/(910 + 30) = 910/940 = 0.968$, so FPR $= 0.032$. It looks excellent because 910 true negatives dominate the denominator. That is the same effect that can make ROC curves look rosy under imbalance.

questions.prompt:
A classifier is scored on 1,000 cases:

|   | Predicted positive | Predicted negative |
|---|---|---|
| Actual positive | 45 | 15 |
| Actual negative | 30 | 910 |

A missed positive (FN) costs USD 500 and a false alarm (FP) costs USD 20. Correct predictions cost nothing. What is the total cost of this model's errors on these 1,000 cases? Give an integer in USD.
questions.explanation: Cost $= 15\times500 + 30\times20 = 7500 + 600 = 8100$. The 15 misses account for over 90% of the cost. That tells you to move the threshold toward higher recall, even at the price of more false alarms.

questions.prompt:
Six test cases, sorted by model score from highest to lowest:

| Score | 0.9 | 0.8 | 0.7 | 0.6 | 0.4 | 0.2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| True label | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |

ROC-AUC equals the fraction of (positive, negative) pairs in which the positive has the higher score. Compute ROC-AUC. Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: There are $3\times3 = 9$ pairs. The positive at 0.9 beats all 3 negatives. The positive at 0.7 beats the negatives at 0.4 and 0.2 (2). The positive at 0.6 beats the same two (2). That gives $7/9 = 0.778$. The only mistakes are the negative at 0.8 outranking two positives.

questions.prompt: Four predictions with true labels $y = [1, 0, 1, 0]$ and predicted probabilities $\hat p = [0.9, 0.2, 0.6, 0.3]$. Compute log loss, $-\text{mean}(y\ln\hat p + (1-y)\ln(1-\hat p))$, using natural logs. Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: Per-case losses: $-\ln 0.9 = 0.105$, $-\ln 0.8 = 0.223$, $-\ln 0.6 = 0.511$, $-\ln 0.7 = 0.357$. Sum $= 1.196$, mean $= 0.299$. Each negative uses $1-\hat p$, the probability given to the true class. Using $\hat p$ for the negatives is the usual slip.

questions.prompt: Same four cases: $y = [1, 0, 1, 0]$, $\hat p = [0.9, 0.2, 0.6, 0.3]$. The Brier score is the mean squared error of the probabilities, $\text{mean}((\hat p - y)^2)$. Compute it. Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: Squared errors: $(0.9-1)^2 = 0.01$, $(0.2-0)^2 = 0.04$, $(0.6-1)^2 = 0.16$, $(0.3-0)^2 = 0.09$. Mean $= 0.30/4 = 0.075$. Like log loss, lower is better and it scores the probabilities themselves. It punishes a confident miss far less harshly than log loss does.

questions.prompt: Targets $y = [10, 12, 8, 15]$ and predictions $\hat y = [11, 12, 6, 12]$. Compute the RMSE. Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: Errors are $-1, 0, 2, 3$. Squares: $1, 0, 4, 9$, mean $3.5$. RMSE $= \sqrt{3.5} = 1.871$. MAE is $(1+0+2+3)/4 = 1.5$. RMSE sits above MAE because squaring weights the error of 3 more heavily.

questions.prompt: A retailer forecasts daily units sold per store and product. Many product-days sell zero units. They want an error metric that is easy to explain and not dominated by a few large misses. Which fits best?
options: MAPE
RMSE
MAE
questions.explanation: MAPE divides by the true value, so any day with $y = 0$ breaks it. RMSE is pulled up by large errors. $R^2$ is a ratio, not an error in units. MAE is in units sold and less sensitive to outliers. MAPE is the tempting pick because percentages are easy to explain, but the zeros rule it out.

questions.prompt: 10,000 transactions contain 50 frauds. Model A predicts "not fraud" every time. Model B catches 40 of the 50 frauds. What is the largest number of false positives B can make and still have accuracy **at least** as high as A's? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: A is right on the 9,950 legitimate cases, so accuracy is 0.995. B gets 40 true positives plus $9{,}950 - FP$ true negatives. Requiring $40 + 9950 - FP \ge 9950$ gives $FP \le 40$. A model that catches 80% of fraud with 41 false alarms has **lower** accuracy than one that catches nothing. That is the accuracy paradox in numbers.

questions.prompt: A model reports precision 0.90 and F1 0.60. What is its recall? Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation: From $F1 = 2PR/(P+R)$: $F1(P+R) = 2PR$, so $R = F1\cdot P/(2P - F1) = 0.6\times0.9/(1.8 - 0.6) = 0.54/1.2 = 0.45$. The arithmetic mean of 0.90 and 0.45 would be 0.675. The harmonic mean pulls F1 down toward the weaker number.

questions.prompt:
A churn model is evaluated on a set with 100 actual churners. A missed churner (FN) costs USD 200. An unneeded retention offer (FP) costs USD 10.

| Threshold | TP | FP |
|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 60 | 40 |
| 0.3 | 80 | 150 |
| 0.2 | 90 | 400 |

What is the lowest total error cost among these three thresholds? Give an integer in USD.
questions.explanation: FN $= 100 - TP$. At 0.5: $40\times200 + 40\times10 = 8400$. At 0.3: $20\times200 + 150\times10 = 5500$. At 0.2: $10\times200 + 400\times10 = 6000$. The minimum is USD 5,500 at 0.3. Dropping to 0.2 saves USD 2,000 in misses (10 more churners caught) but adds USD 2,500 in offers (250 more false positives).

questions.prompt: A screening test set has 100 positives and 100,000 negatives. At one threshold the model has recall 0.80 and false positive rate 0.02, a point that looks excellent on the ROC curve. What is the precision at that threshold? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: $TP = 0.80\times100 = 80$. $FP = 0.02\times100{,}000 = 2{,}000$. Precision $= 80/2080 = 0.038$. That is 25 false alarms for every true case caught. FPR divides by the huge negative count, so it hides 2,000 false positives. Precision does not, which is why PR-AUC is the more honest choice for rare events.

questions.prompt: Five cases: $y = [1, 1, 0, 0, 1]$ and $\hat p = [0.8, 0.7, 0.1, 0.99, 0.6]$. Compute the log loss (natural logs). Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: Losses: $-\ln0.8 = 0.223$, $-\ln0.7 = 0.357$, $-\ln0.9 = 0.105$, $-\ln0.01 = 4.605$, $-\ln0.6 = 0.511$. Sum $= 5.801$, mean $= 1.160$. The fourth case is a negative predicted at 0.99, so its loss is $-\ln(1-0.99) = 4.605$. That one confident mistake is 79% of the total. Without it the other four average only 0.299. Log loss punishes confident wrong predictions heavily.

questions.prompt: A model's absolute errors on 10 test cases are nine errors of 1 and one error of 21. Compute the ratio RMSE / MAE. Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation: MAE $= (9\times1 + 21)/10 = 3$. MSE $= (9\times1 + 441)/10 = 45$, so RMSE $= \sqrt{45} = 6.708$. Ratio $= 6.708/3 = 2.24$. That is above the rule-of-thumb value of 2, so outliers are driving RMSE. Here one bad case produces most of the squared error.

questions.prompt: A disease classifier is validated on a balanced set (50% positive). It has recall 0.80 and false positive rate 0.05, so precision there is $0.40/(0.40 + 0.025) = 0.941$. It is deployed on a population where 1% of people have the disease. Recall and FPR stay the same. What precision should you expect? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: Per person: true positives $0.80\times0.01 = 0.008$. False positives $0.05\times0.99 = 0.0495$. Precision $= 0.008/0.0575 = 0.139$. Recall and FPR are rates within each class, so they carry over. Precision depends on the base rate, which is Bayes' theorem from Chapter 3. A 0.94 precision on a balanced test set says little about a rare-disease deployment.

questions.prompt: A model's probabilities are well calibrated. A false negative costs USD 500 and a false positive costs USD 20. Flagging a case with probability $p$ has expected cost $(1-p)\times20$. Not flagging it has expected cost $p\times500$. Above what probability threshold should you flag? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: Flag when $p\times500 > (1-p)\times20$, so $p > 20/(20 + 500) = 0.0385$. The general rule is $t^* = C_{FP}/(C_{FP} + C_{FN})$. The default 0.5 is only optimal when both errors cost the same. This rule only holds if $p$ is a real probability, which is why calibration matters when probabilities drive a decision.

questions.prompt: A gradient-boosted model has ROC-AUC 0.92. Its reliability diagram is S-shaped: overconfident near 0 and 1. You apply Platt scaling, which passes the scores through a fitted, increasing sigmoid. Select ALL statements that are correct.
options: Fitting the calibrator on the test set and then scoring the test set gives an honest estimate of calibration
Log loss can improve, because confident wrong predictions become less extreme
The high ROC-AUC already showed the probabilities were trustworthy, so calibration was optional
ROC-AUC stays the same, because an increasing transform keeps the ranking of cases
questions.explanation: ROC-AUC depends only on the order of the scores, and an increasing map keeps that order. Log loss scores the probabilities, so shrinking overconfident extremes can cut it sharply. High ROC-AUC measures discrimination, not calibration. Fitting the calibrator on the data you score it on is leakage. Use `CalibratedClassifierCV` with cross-validation on the training data, as in Listing 16.4.

questions.prompt: A "baseline" forecaster always predicts the **training** mean, 8. The test targets are $[10, 12, 14]$. What is $R^2$ on the test set? Give a decimal to 1 d.p.
questions.explanation: $SS_{res} = (10-8)^2 + (12-8)^2 + (14-8)^2 = 4 + 16 + 36 = 56$. The test mean is 12, so $SS_{tot} = 4 + 0 + 4 = 8$. $R^2 = 1 - 56/8 = -6.0$. $R^2 = 0$ is the score of predicting the **test** mean. A constant from the training data scores below 0 whenever the target has shifted, which is common with drift or a time-based split.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the confusion matrix definitions, explain in one sentence each what a false positive and a false negative mean for a spam filter, and state which one is more costly there.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A false positive is a legitimate email wrongly flagged as spam: annoying, since a real message gets buried, but rarely dangerous. A false negative is actual spam that gets through to the inbox: usually mildly annoying and cheap, though a phishing email that gets through can be costly. Between the two, false positives are generally treated as more costly for a spam filter. Losing a legitimate email, a job offer, a bill, can have real consequences, while an occasional spam message reaching the inbox is a minor inconvenience.

bookExercises.prompt: State which metric (precision, recall, or F1) is most appropriate for: (a) a disease-screening test; (b) a spam filter; (c) a general-purpose classifier comparison with no stated cost asymmetry.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: (a) Recall: missing a real disease case (false negative) is the costly error in screening. (b) Precision: flagging a legitimate email as spam (false positive) is the costly error. (c) F1: with no stated cost asymmetry, a balanced single metric is the reasonable default for general comparison.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 16.5, compute precision and recall by hand from TN=41, FP=1, FN=1, TP=71, and confirm they match the reported 0.9861 figures.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Precision $= TP/(TP+FP) = 71/(71+1) = 71/72 \approx 0.9861$. Recall $= TP/(TP+FN) = 71/(71+1) = 71/72 \approx 0.9861$. Both match the reported figures. In this case, precision and recall come out numerically equal because FP and FN happen to both equal 1 on this particular test set.

bookExercises.prompt: Using this chapter's hypothetical 0.1%-fraud scenario, compute the accuracy of a model that predicts "fraud" for every transaction instead (the opposite extreme), and state its precision and recall.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A model predicting "fraud" for every transaction in the 0.1%-fraud scenario would be correct only on the 0.1% that are fraud, giving accuracy $\approx 0.001$ (0.1%), catastrophically low. Precision would be $TP/(TP+FP) = 0.001$, since only 0.1% of its "fraud" calls are actually fraud. Recall would be $1.0$: it catches every real fraud case, trivially, by flagging everything. This is the mirror-image failure mode to the "always predict not-fraud" model: perfect recall bought at the cost of near-total precision collapse.

bookExercises.prompt: A customer reports "our fraud model has 99.9% accuracy" as evidence it's ready to ship. Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say before agreeing.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "99.9% accuracy on a fraud dataset where fraud is rare is close to what you'd get by predicting 'not fraud' every single time. Accuracy alone can't distinguish a good model from a completely useless one under this kind of imbalance. Before agreeing it's ready, I'd want to see recall and precision (or PR-AUC) specifically on the fraud class, since those are the numbers that actually say whether it catches real fraud."

bookExercises.prompt: A Random Forest's `predict_proba` output is being used directly to set insurance premiums. Using this chapter's Calibration section, explain what could go wrong and what you'd check before trusting those numbers.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Random Forests are a common source of S-shaped miscalibration, under-confident at the extremes. A `predict_proba` of 0.75 might correspond to an observed positive rate closer to 0.9. Using such probabilities directly to set premiums risks systematically mispricing risk at the extremes: charging too little for the genuinely high-risk cases, and too much for the lowest-risk ones. Before trusting the numbers, plot a reliability diagram (Procedure 16.4). If it deviates from the diagonal, apply `CalibratedClassifierCV` with isotonic regression before using the probabilities for pricing.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the Davis and Goadrich (2006) paper's abstract. Identify the specific claim it makes about ROC curves under class imbalance, and explain how it relates to this chapter's PR-AUC recommendation for rare-event detection.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. Davis and Goadrich's core claim is that ROC curves can present an overly optimistic picture of classifier performance specifically under class imbalance. The false positive rate, the ROC curve's x-axis, is normalised by the large number of true negatives, making even a fairly high absolute count of false positives look small. Precision, the PR curve's y-axis, is by contrast directly sensitive to that same false positive count relative to total positive predictions. This is exactly why this chapter recommends PR-AUC over ROC-AUC for rare-event detection: PR-AUC doesn't get the same optimistic distortion from an abundance of true negatives.
